walkthroughs.body_html:
Coursework: Personal Response — a core area of A-Level English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coursework: Personal Response brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Coursework: Personal Response.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why does historical context matter when reading literature?
options: Context just means writing about what the author had for breakfast.
Dystopian fiction predicts what will actually happen in 100 years.
Texts emerge from and respond to specific historical conditions — context illuminates references, assumptions and arguments that might otherwise be invisible.
Context is required because all texts are about history.

mcqs.q: What is the function of dystopian fiction?
options: Dystopian fiction predicts what will actually happen in 100 years.
Context is required because all texts are about history.
To critique tendencies in the writer's own society by extrapolating them into a nightmarish future — dystopias hold up a warning mirror to the present.
Dystopian fiction is just storytelling set in scary futures.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.
Dystopian fiction predicts what will actually happen in 100 years.
A theme is the title of the book.
